Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-18
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 48m (approx)
Attendees: Aisha Kapoor (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Balakrishnan (CTO, Nimbus Health), Tom Reyes (Senior ML Eng), Sofia Alvarez (Product Lead)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Redwood gave a hosted API walkthrough focusing on real-time chat streaming, recommended parameter settings, and retry/fallback patterns. Customer is evaluating latency and cost tradeoffs for embedding chat into their telehealth triage flow. Security and data residency questions were raised; next steps include pricing, streaming code samples, and an on-prem/dedicated scoping conversation.

Topics covered:
- Hosted API quickstart and Console tour
- Streaming vs polling behavior and how tokens stream back
- Parameter tuning: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop sequences, presence/penalty hints
- Retry/backoff strategies, idempotency, and partial response handling
- Cost/latency tradeoffs and caching prefixes
- Security (SSO, KMS, audit logs) and dedicated/private deployment options

Action items (captured in metadata too)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 45 minutes. Quick round—who's on from Nimbus?
[00:06] Priya: Hi, Priya here. I'm the CTO. We'll mostly be listening; Tom and Sofia are going to ask the deep technical and product questions.
[00:11] Tom: Hey all. Hi Aisha, Liam.
[00:13] Sofia: Hello.
[00:15] Aisha: Great. Liam, do you want to take us through the hosted demo and streaming behavior?
[00:19] Liam: Yeah sure. I'll share my screen—give me one sec.
[00:31] Liam: Alright, screen's up. So quick agenda: show the Console for a hosted model, then live API demo streaming a chat, then parameter tweaks and retry patterns. We'll also point out where Optimize suggests batching and caching.
[00:45] Liam: First, Console view—model catalog. We support a catalog of open and verified models and the latency/cost estimates per 1k tokens. You can pin model versions at route level, so production won't drift.
[00:59] Priya: When you say "pin" — is that per environment? We have stage/prod separation and strict change control.
[01:04] Liam: Yes, you can have route-level pins and rollout policies — canary or gradual. The Console shows active rollouts and the token-level cost breakdown.
[01:13] Aisha: Quick question from our side: what's your latency SLO you want to target? 
[01:18] Priya: For triage flow, we'd like 300–500ms tail for short prompts, and under 1.5s for longer back-and-forths. Cost is also a factor; we want to avoid 10x spend.
[01:29] Liam: Good to know. For 300–500ms tail that's typically a smaller model or a quantized variant on dedicated hardware. On hosted we hit mid-low ms for small prompts but it depends on concurrency.
[01:39] Liam: Now the live example: I'm going to call the /v1/chat/completions endpoint using streaming. You get a chunked response where each data: chunk has a delta. This approach reduces perceived latency because the front end can render partial tokens.
[01:55] [02:00] Liam: (typing sound) Example prompt: "Patient reports chest discomfort and shortness of breath, triage suggestions and next steps."
[02:12] Liam: You'll see the UI render tokens as they arrive. If streaming stalls we recommend a client-side timer to show progress — not to be confused with retries.
[02:23] Tom: How do you handle partial responses if a retry kicks in mid-stream? We don't want duplicate or truncated notes saved to the patient chart.
[02:31] Liam: Good question. Two recommended patterns: 1) Use idempotency keys for each user-turn so retries don't create duplicate server-side entries. 2) Have the client buffer the streamed tokens and submit the full assembled message once the server indicates completion.
[02:46] Priya: Idempotency keys — are those at the Redwood request level or do we need to implement our own?
[02:50] Liam: Redwood accepts an idempotency header (we'll share the exact header name) and will handle dedup on our side for the same request ID within a time window. But for streaming partials you should still assemble and checkpoint client-side — we don't want semantically half-committed updates.
[03:05] Liam: Also we support a synchronous fallback: if streaming fails, you can re-call with the same request ID and set a flag to return a non-streaming full completion. That way the client can switch modes cleanly.
[03:18] Sofia: If we switch to non-streaming mid-turn, do we lose the prefix cache benefits?
[03:23] Liam: We'll try to keep the prefix in cache for a short TTL. But switching modes may change how we batch, so latencies can differ.
[03:31] Aisha: Let's demo parameter impacts. Liam, show temperature / max_tokens changes.
[03:34] Liam: Yep. Here's a short prompt; temperature 0.0 vs 0.7. With temp 0.0 you get deterministic replies — good for standard triage recommendations. With 0.7 it's more diverse — maybe useful for content synthesis but not for clinical notes.
[03:50] [04:00] Liam: max_tokens — set a strict cap if you want to bound cost. Also top_p gives nucleus sampling. For our customers building templates, we often recommend a low temperature and explicit stop sequences to avoid hallucinated disclaimers.
[04:18] Tom: Any built-in safety classifiers? We need to detect PHI leakage and content policy violations in user prompts.
[04:24] Liam: On the hosted side we have optional pre- and post-processing hooks. You can run sanitized checks in a middleware layer before sending tokens. We can also show how to route sensitive prompts to Dedicated or Private deployments to limit egress.
[04:36] Priya: That's important. We cannot have PHI leaving controls. What's the recommended path?
[04:40] Aisha: For regulated PHI you likely need Private or Dedicated with VPC and KMS integration. We'll include the security whitepaper and SOC2 evidence.
[04:51] [05:00] Liam: Back to retries. We recommend an exponential backoff with jitter: try quick short retries for transient 5xx, fallback to a non-streaming call after N attempts, and as a last resort use a smaller model on a different route as a graceful degradation.
[05:17] Tom: How do you signal partial success to the user? E.g., if we get useful first-paragraph guidance but the rest times out.
[05:22] Liam: UI patterns: show "partial answer" tag and persist the assembled partial response locally (not to primary chart) until the final is confirmed. Server-side, use the request status so you can reconcile later.
[05:33] Sofia: Can Optimize suggest batching settings automatically? We saw a note in docs about Optimize recommending cacheable prefixes.
[05:38] Liam: Yes, Optimize looks at token distributions and suggests batching windows and cache TTLs per route. For triage flows where many prompts share the same opening context (patient demographics + history), prefix caching can reduce cost materially.
[05:52] [06:00] Aisha: Let's show an SDK snippet for streaming + retry. Liam, can you paste the JS example?
[06:05] Liam: (pastes code) The key bits: set stream: true; attach an onData handler to append deltas; if connection drops, call reconnect logic with same idempotency key; if retries exceed 2, fall back to non-streaming.
[06:23] Liam: I'll read a truncated example: "const resp = await client.chat.create({ model: 'rwd-chat-1', messages, stream: true, idempotencyKey });" Then a loop that listens for chunk events.
[06:37] Tom: What about token accounting during streaming if we abort mid-stream — are those tokens billed?
[06:42] Liam: Billing is per token generated by the model. If the model generated tokens before the abort, those are billed. We have a preview meters column in the Console so you can estimate. Also caching/prefix reuse reduces generated tokens overall.
[06:56] Priya: Would we be able to set token budget per user session in the Console? We want to limit cost exposure for large sessions.
[07:01] Liam: You can set per-route quotas and token limits; also implement throttling per user on your side. Redwood can enforce quotas via API keys and route configs.
[07:12] [07:30] Sofia: About function/tool calling — do you support structured tool outputs for downstream ingestion?
[07:34] Liam: Yes, we support a function-calling pattern where the model returns JSON schema-conformant payloads. That's useful for composing actions like "schedule follow-up" or populate EHR fields. We do caution on strict schema validation.
[07:48] Tom: Any gotchas when using function calling with streaming?
[07:52] Liam: Streaming and function-calling mix ok if you design for chunk assembly. Typically you stream the content, detect the function call marker, and then parse the assembled payload after completion. If you need stronger guarantees, use a synchronous call for the function stage.
[08:07] [08:30] Aisha: Time check—~40 minutes left? Sorry, math. We have about 35 left. Quick security note: Priya asked about KMS and audit logs. Liam?
[08:40] Liam: We integrate with customer-managed KMS for Dedicated and Private. Hosted uses our KMS but supports encryption at rest and TLS in transit. Audit logs for API calls and model versions are available and can be exported to your SIEM. We'll attach the security brief.
[08:58] Priya: Are audit logs accessible from Console?
[09:01] Liam: Yes, Console has an audit view and you can stream logs to your cloud. For high-compliance customers we also offer a private control plane.
[09:10] Tom: For PII we need data retention controls. Can we set retention windows and auto-purge?
[09:15] Aisha: Yes, retention policies can be configured for Dedicated/Private. On hosted we have configurable retention and redaction policies but some customers prefer Private for guaranteed on-prem retention.
[09:27] [09:45] Liam: Back to retries: example sequence: initial streaming attempt -> failure at T+1s -> client waits 200ms jittered -> retry with same idempotency key -> server either returns continuation or a new completion. If retries fail, call non-streaming on fallback. We also recommend logging attempt metrics in Console for per-route analysis.
[10:05] Tom: Does Redwood provide SDK-level helpers for reconnection/resume so we don't reimplement complex logic?
[10:10] Liam: We provide example helpers but not a complete reconnection state machine yet. We'll share a helper snippet that is robust for most cases. It's in the SDK recipes in our docs.
[10:19] Sofia: On cost, if we move to Dedicated, do we still pay per token?
[10:23] Liam: Dedicated is commit-based; token pricing is lower and there's a monthly commitment for GPU capacity. We'll include the different cost buckets in the pricing doc.
[10:33] [10:45] Aisha: Let's role play a failure scenario quickly — Liam can simulate a transient 5xx during streaming.
[10:51] Liam: Ok hitting the endpoint... (simulated) Response: connection reset after 700ms. Client shows partial tokens. Our demo helper kicks in: waits 250ms, retry, got a 200 with final tokens, stitched and deduped.
[11:08] Tom: Looks good. In our product we have to make sure partials aren't stored to patient record until final ACK.
[11:14] Liam: Right — client should mark partials as ephemeral until completion. Also store request IDs so you can dedupe on server side.
[11:22] Priya: On the security docs — we need an ISO/SOC2 summary and the option for a private control plane.
[11:28] Aisha: We'll include SOC2 and the Private deployment brief. For next step let's get a bench test scheduled.
[11:36] [11:45] Sofia: One more quick SDK question: Do you have TypeScript typings for streaming events?
[11:50] Liam: Yes, typings are available in the SDK and the repo includes an example consumer. We'll link it.
[11:57] Tom: We'll probably run a small POC: onboarding 5 clinicians, 1k sessions/day for two weeks.
[12:03] Aisha: Great. We'll prepare a scope doc and recommended routes and model variants.
[12:10] [12:30] Closing recap:
Aisha: Recap — Redwood to send pricing + dedicated options + security docs; Liam to share streaming retry code snippets and SDK helpers; Tom to provide sample prompts and dataset; schedule bench test for week of 9/22.
[12:44] Priya: Sounds good, thanks.
[12:46] Tom: Thanks all.
[12:47] Aisha: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up.
